clue.text: First of the common people, this woodcutter with a Finnish friend

parts.note: the stock phrase for ordinary folk is Tom, Dick and Harry, so Tom comes first
a sawyer is someone who saws timber

explanation.surface: A lumberjack, the most ordinary of men, has a pal from Finland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finnish' is a pun: the friend is Huckleberry Finn, not a native of Finland. Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's boy hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain's boy hero has Huckleberry Finn as his closest companion.

clue.text: Original metal worker changes into a lab tunic

indicators.note: the letters of the clue's last three words change their order to make a new word

explanation.surface: An ancient smith swaps his apron for a laboratory coat.
explanation.walkthrough: Tubal-cain, in Genesis, is the first forger of bronze and iron, hence 'original'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis this descendant of Cain is the first craftsman in bronze and iron, so the earliest smith.

clue.text: Sophie was the last glowing one

definitions.text: Sophie was the last glowing one

parts.words: Sophie was the last glowing one
parts.note: the singer Sophie Tucker was billed as 'The Last of the Red-Hot' ones of this kind; glowing stands for red-hot

explanation.surface: A woman called Sophie was the final ember still burning.
explanation.walkthrough: Sophie Tucker, the American vaudeville star, was billed as 'The Last of the Red-Hot Mamas'; 'glowing' stands in for red-hot.
explanation.definitionFit: An American spelling of mother, as in Sophie Tucker's billing as a red-hot entertainer.

clue.text: A striker kicking up a row in the butchery centre

parts.note: a bat is something you strike a ball with

indicators.note: in a down clue, kicking up turns the word for a row so it reads upwards

parts.note: a riot is a noisy disturbance, a row

explanation.surface: A footballer causes a disturbance in the middle of a meat-cutting area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kicking up' reverses RIOT to TOIR, which follows A and BAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A slaughterhouse is the place where animals are butchered.

clue.text: Mountainous singer, often head vocalist

parts.note: an Alpine performer who sings among mountains and flips between chest and head voice

explanation.surface: A huge vocalist is frequently the band's lead singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountainous' looks like a description of size; it means from the mountains. 'Head vocalist' is not a lead singer but one using the falsetto head voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpine singing breaks rapidly between chest voice and falsetto head voice.

clue.text: Withdraw to change suit unnecessarily

definitions.meaning: to take back or cancel, as a licence or an order
in card games, to play a card of another suit when one could have followed suit

explanation.surface: Someone backs out rather than swap clothes without need.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge and whist a revoke is the offence of not following suit when able to.
explanation.definitionFit: Cancelling a decree is one sense; the other is the card-table offence of failing to follow suit.

clue.text: Test of vehicle condition — that's the big idea

parts.note: the MOT is the annual British roadworthiness test for cars
if introduces a condition

explanation.surface: Passing your car's roadworthiness inspection is the main thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is the yearly safety check every older car in Britain must pass. 'Test of vehicle condition' reads as one phrase but splits after 'vehicle'.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring theme in a work of art is its dominant or central idea.

clue.text: Part of frieze in opera house almost uncovered

parts.note: the Met is the Metropolitan Opera in New York

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word for uncovered is lost

parts.note: open means not covered

explanation.surface: A section of decorative band in a theatre has been nearly exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of OPEN to give OPE.
explanation.definitionFit: In a Doric frieze the square panels between the triglyphs are called by this name.

clue.text: Clement met Peter outside a resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort: sort the letters of these words again into a new order

explanation.surface: Clement and Peter had a meeting outside a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town but is the anagram signal, re-sort. 'Clement' looks like a man's name; it is the adjective meaning mild.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement weather is mild, neither too hot nor too cold.

clue.text: The end in France is also the end in England

parts.note: fin is French for end
taken as written

explanation.surface: The final word in French means the same in English.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin finis, written at the close of books, is used in English for the end.
explanation.definitionFit: English printers borrowed the Latin word for a conclusion to mark the last page of a book.

clue.text: Dreary rabble in retreat — attack with artillery

indicators.note: an army in retreat goes backwards, so the words for dreary and rabble are read backwards together

parts.note: drab means dull or dreary
a mob is a disorderly crowd

explanation.surface: A dull crowd falls back while big guns open fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' reverses DRAB MOB as a whole to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelling a position with heavy guns is a sustained artillery assault.

clue.text: For nutrition take wine, swallowing it before noon

indicators.note: the word for wine takes in, as if swallowing, the other pieces

parts.note: vin is French for wine, familiar from vin rouge
a.m. stands for ante meridiem, before midday

explanation.surface: To stay healthy have a drink, gulping it down in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallowing' puts IT and AM inside VIN.
explanation.definitionFit: These organic compounds are essential parts of a diet, taken for good nourishment.

clue.text: Inclined to speak fast

indicators.note: the word for a fast is spoken and heard as a different spelling

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: Someone tends to talk rapidly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like speed but is a period of abstinence.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of lean: tilted or tended towards something.

clue.text: Mere versifiers like Southey

parts.note: a mere is a lake, a sense common in English place names
poets write verse

explanation.surface: Robert Southey and his kind were mere rhymesters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mere' looks like the adjective 'only'; it is a lake. Southey, Wordsworth and Coleridge lived in the English Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Southey belonged with Wordsworth and Coleridge to the group of Romantic poets in Cumbria.

clue.text: Records by pre-eminent composer

parts.note: arch as a prefix means chief or principal, as in archbishop
Charles Ives was an American composer

explanation.surface: Documents left by a leading composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' joins the two pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical documents kept in a repository are collectively its records.

clue.text: This is associated with a political outsider like Gladstone

definitions.text: This is associated with a political outsider like Gladstone

parts.words: This is associated with a political outsider like Gladstone
parts.note: a travelling bag gave its name to Northern opportunists in the post-Civil War South; a Gladstone is also a type of bag

explanation.surface: Something linked with a statesman like Gladstone who was not part of the establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gladstone' looks like the prime minister but is a Gladstone bag. In the US a carpetbagger was a Northerner who went South after the Civil War for political gain.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth travelling bag gave its name to opportunist political incomers, and a Gladstone is another kind of travelling bag.

clue.text: Some barmaids remove the froth

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following word are used

explanation.surface: A few women behind the bar skim off the head of the beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Barm is the froth on fermenting malt liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: Barm is the foam that forms on top of fermenting beer.

clue.text: Lead astray girl said to be still at school

indicators.note: the word for a girl is heard, its spelling differing from what is written

parts.note: miss is a title for an unmarried girl
a pupil still at school is in a form, a school class

explanation.surface: Lead a young woman astray who apparently has not left school yet.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class, so a pupil 'in form' is still at school.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone wrong information leads them into error.

clue.text: There is a limit to the effrontery of Whitey

parts.note: a pale is a boundary, as in beyond the pale
face can mean cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: There is only so much cheek a white man will take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whitey' is a slang word for a white person.
explanation.definitionFit: A term attributed to Native Americans in westerns for a white person.

clue.text: Drink one ferments in cask

parts.note: punch is a mixed drink

indicators.note: fermenting stirs things up, so the letters of 'one' are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drink is fermenting inside a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ferments' rearranges ONE to EON.
explanation.definitionFit: A large barrel for wine or beer, holding about seventy gallons.

clue.text: Annoy a spy

definitions.meaning: a police informer, in British slang

explanation.surface: Irritate an agent.
explanation.walkthrough: As a British slang verb it means to irritate; as a noun it means a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for irritating someone, and also for a copper's informant.

clue.text: Wrongly accused university staff of messengers

indicators.note: the letters are put together wrongly, out of order

explanation.surface: Campus employees in the post room are unjustly blamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees but is a rod. 'Wrongly' rearranges ACCUSED plus U.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged rod with twin snakes was carried by Hermes and other heralds of the gods.

clue.text: You can get killed, going for a tackle like this

definitions.text: You can get killed, going for a tackle like this

parts.words: You can get killed, going for a tackle like this
parts.note: RAF slang for being killed is going for one of these, and the word also names a kind of lifting tackle

explanation.surface: A footballer risks death by making a reckless challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone for a Burton' was RAF slang in the Second World War for killed. 'tackle' looks like football but is a pulley system.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hoisting tackle on ships bears this name, as does the wartime phrase for someone killed.

clue.text: It's crazy, calling out name in French

indicators.note: crazy means wildly disordered, so the remaining letters are jumbled
out means the letter for name is left out of the word

explanation.surface: Shouting out someone's name in the French language is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes N from CALLING, and 'crazy' scrambles CALLIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallic is the adjective for France and its people, from Gaul.

clue.text: Theorize about the making of Capulet's enmity originally

indicators.note: about signals that the letters are moved around

parts.note: Capulet is Juliet's family in Romeo and Juliet

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of the word enmity

explanation.surface: Speculate on how the Capulets' feud with the Montagues first began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges CAPULETS plus E, the first letter of 'enmity'.
explanation.definitionFit: To speculate is to form a theory without firm evidence.

clue.text: Scout meal

definitions.meaning: to dismiss scornfully, as in scouting an idea

explanation.surface: A Boy Scout's dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scout' looks like a Boy Scout but is the old verb meaning to reject with scorn.
explanation.definitionFit: To mock or jeer, and also informal for food.

clue.text: Shelter for black-hearted murderer

indicators.note: hearted means put at the heart, so the letter for black goes in the middle

parts.note: Cain killed his brother Abel
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A refuge for an evil-minded killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black-hearted' reads as wicked but puts B at the heart of CAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A hut or small house gives basic shelter.

clue.text: "Grishkin … gives promise of pneumatic —" (T.S.Eliot)

parts.note: the missing last word of a line from Eliot's Whispers of Immortality, about Grishkin's uncorseted bust

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from T.S. Eliot's 'Whispers of Immortality': 'Uncorseted, her friendly bust / Gives promise of pneumatic bliss.'
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's line ends on perfect happiness, the joy Grishkin's figure promises.

clue.text: This is said without restraint about the ring road

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for said goes round the other

parts.note: oral means spoken
a bit is the mouthpiece that restrains a horse

explanation.surface: A road round a town is described as having no speed limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without restraint' reads as freely, but 'without' means outside: ORAL goes round BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A British road encircling a town is called an orbital, as with the M25 round London.

clue.text: One note recurring in Italian river poet

indicators.note: in places the reversed pieces inside the river's name

parts.note: the Arno flows through Florence and Pisa

indicators.note: recurring here means running back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A single musical note keeps coming back to a poet by a river in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurring' reverses I and TE to give ETI, which goes inside ARNO. Pietro Aretino was a Renaissance Italian poet and satirist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pietro Aretino was a sixteenth-century Italian writer of satirical verse.

clue.text: Dickensian fellow is gettin' on

parts.note: getting on means ageing, and the dropped g in the clue invites the casual spelling agin'

explanation.surface: A character from Dickens is growing old.
explanation.walkthrough: Fagin is the old receiver of stolen goods in Oliver Twist. The clue's 'gettin'' signals that 'ageing' loses its g too.
explanation.definitionFit: Fagin is a character from Oliver Twist, a creation of Dickens.

clue.text: Straight silk dress, low cut

parts.note: a close-fitting Chinese silk dress, high-collared but slit up the side so cut low on the leg

explanation.surface: A simple silk gown with a plunging neckline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low cut' suggests a plunging neckline; this dress has a high collar and is cut low at the skirt with a side slit.
explanation.definitionFit: The close-fitting Chinese gown with a mandarin collar and side slits is traditionally made of silk.
